info.bio: The Pretenders es un grupo anglo-americano de rock que en sus comienzos (1978) formó parte de la llamada new wave. La banda se componía originalmente de su fundadora, compositora, guitarrista y vocalista Chrissie Hynde, el guitarrista James Honeyman-Scott, el bajista Pete Farndon y el batería Martin Chambers. Las muertes de Honeyman-Scott y Farndon por consumo de drogas malograron esta formación, y los múltiples cambios de músicos en los años

scenes.desc: American Graffiti (1973) desata el revival de los cincuenta y sesenta, que suenan más auténticos que el rock corporativo de los setenta: rockabilly, surf, folk-rock, psicodelia, bandas sonoras de terror. Los punks descubren el alma malvada del rockabilly: Suicide inventa el psychobilly y los Cramps el «voodoobilly»; Fleshtones, Raybeats, Stray Cats, Von Lmo. El garage revive con Slickee Boys, Pretenders, Wipers, Real Kids; el power-pop con Cheap Trick, Shoes, Cars, Jonathan Richman y Embarrassment. En California, los Blasters y el cow-punk de Rank And File; Tom Petty como teórico del power-pop, Plimsouls, Redd Kross, Go-Go's, Bangles. El blues para la generación punk: George Thorogood, Fabulous Thunderbirds, J. Geils Band, Dixie Dregs.

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde's Kent State Experience (May 4, 1970)
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde was a student at Kent State University on May 4, 1970, when the shootings occurred. She witnessed the events, knew one of the students who was killed, and vividly recalled hearing the shots and being carried off campus. Her memories also include the burning down of the ROTC building by students in protest of the Cambodia invasion, and the presence of both ROTC members (teenagers given loaded rifles) and the Ohio National Guard. "Well, yes. They killed four people and they closed down the university and the National Guard were surrounding a building which we, the student body, had burnt down a few days earlier in a protest when Nixon invaded Cambodia."

podcast.title: Inspiration from Kent State (1970)
podcast.body: The killings at Kent State profoundly affected Chrissie Hynde, leading her to drop out of school and abandon her plans for an art degree. Although she initially drifted, the experience eventually set her on a path that led to her career as a rock star. "It would be inaccurate to say that the killings at Kent State led Chrissy Hine to rock and roll. Many may have put her on the path because she dropped out of school and abandoned her plans to get a degree in art after the shootings."

podcast.title: Times Square Soundtrack Contribution (1980)
podcast.body: The Pretenders were among the artists featured on the soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square*. This soundtrack was notable for being one of the very first to showcase the nascent alternative music of the era, introducing a wider audience to punk and new wave. "The soundtrack featured the pretenders, Roxy music, Gary Newman, XTC, Joe Jackson."

podcast.title: Tragic Deaths of Band Members (1982)
podcast.body: Within two years of the band's 1980 debut, two of The Pretenders' four members died. Dick Varnedon was fired due to drug abuse and subsequently died from it on June 14, 1982. Just two days later, James Honeyman-Scott died from heart failure, also brought on by drug abuse, a stark example of the "rock and roll lifestyle's" complications. "Dick Varnedon who was fired because of his drug abuse and died from the same on June 14, 1982. Two days later, James Honeyman Scott died from heart failure brought on by drug abuse."

podcast.title: Neil Young's Rock and Roll Hall of Fame Induction (2005)
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde had the opportunity to thank Neil Young for writing "Ohio" years later. Young returned the gesture by inducting The Pretenders into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2005, an event Hynde could not have imagined as a Kent State student. "But when she and her band, the pretenders were inducted into the rock and roll hall of fame in 2005, Neal Young is the person who did it."

podcast.body: The Pretenders are mentioned in connection with Akron, Ohio, as the original home of Chrissy Hine, which is also the home of The Black Keys and a source of regional influence for Karen O. of The Ye-Eyes. podcast.title: Band Formation Year
podcast.body: The Pretenders finally solidified in 1978 after several earlier attempts by Chrissie Hynde to establish a band. "There were several before the pretenders finally took hold of 1978."

podcast.title: Bridge Between Punk and New Wave
podcast.body: The Pretenders served as an important bridge between the raw energy of punk and the more experimental and artistic leanings of New Wave. Their sound demonstrated how punk's underlying attitude could evolve into new musical forms. "The pretenders were an important bridge between punk and new wave."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bridge Between Punk and New Wave
podcast.body: The Pretenders were considered a crucial bridge, linking the raw energy of old-school punk with the evolving sounds of the New Wave era. "The pretenders were a crucial bridge between old school punk and the era of New Wave."

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde Collaboration
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde, frontwoman of The Pretenders, was one of the artists who collaborated with Taylor Hawkins on his Co-Tale Riders albums. Her involvement underscores the diverse range of musicians Hawkins brought into his side project. "Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders."

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde on Rock Music Simplicity vs. Lifestyle Complexity
podcast.body: In her autobiography, Chrissie Hynde stated that she didn't understand why rock music was considered complicated, seeing it as "just high school dropouts playing three chords." However, she acknowledged that the "rock and roll lifestyle" itself could be very complicated. "In her autobiography, Chrissy Hind said she did not understand what was so complicated about rock music. Really, it's just high school dropouts playing three chords, she said."

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde's Intent for "Brass in Pocket"
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde intended "Brass in Pocket" to be a "real traditional" rock song, aiming for confidence and swagger rather than a feminist statement. She expressed mystification by the focus on the "girl thing" in relation to the song, stating that "tradition in rock is what turns me on." "Chrissy did not intend this to be a feminist anthem. She intended it to be a traditional rock song."

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde's Origins
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde, who would later form The Pretenders, was an American girl who for a while was a member of the London SS, Mick Jones's band before The Clash. This highlights an early connection between key figures in the emerging punk and new wave scenes.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde's Punk Credentials
podcast.body: Singer Chrissie Hynde, originally from Akron, Ohio, moved to London and amassed impeccable punk rock credentials. These included working in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop during the early days of the Sex Pistols, writing about punk in British music magazines, and playing guitar in several short-lived British punk bands, one of which later evolved into The Clash. "Singer Chrissy Hind was from Akron, Ohio of all places, but she had escaped to London. And she had impeccable punk rock credentials."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chrissie Hynde's Punk Credentials
podcast.body: Lead singer Chrissie Hynde, originally from Akron, Ohio, moved to the UK and became deeply involved in the early punk scene, working at Malcolm McLaren's shop "Sex" and playing guitar in bands that morphed into The Clash and The Damned, even considering a marriage of convenience with Sid Vicious. "So yeah, a lot of bonafide punk credentials."

podcast.title: Continued Activity
podcast.body: Despite being nearly 70 years old, Chrissie Hynde remains active in music. "even though she's nearly 70, she is still going."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Influences
podcast.body: From childhood, Chrissie Hynde loved the guitar and, due to a scarcity of female role models, drew inspiration from James Brown's guitarist. She also admired artists like Alice Cooper, The Stooges, and Jeff Beck. "She loved the guitar from the time she was a kid. With few female role models, she looked to the guitarist employed by James Brown. She loved Alice Cooper and the stooages and Jeff Beck."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early MTV Presence
podcast.body: On the first day of MTV's launch, The Pretenders were among the UK-based acts whose multiple clips were played, benefiting from the British heritage of shooting more music videos. "On day one, MTV played multiple clips by such UK-based acts as The Pretenders."

podcast.body: The group dynamic of The Pretenders effectively transitioned into a solo singer situation at one point in their career. "a group might become a solo singer, the police or the pretenders effectively did that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Exotic Appeal
podcast.body: The fact that three-quarters of The Pretenders' members were English contributed to the band's somewhat exotic appeal, adding a distinctive touch to their image and sound within the New Wave landscape. "Add in the fact that the pretenders were three quarters English, also gave them a somewhat exotic touch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fighting Sexism and Becoming a Role Model
podcast.body: Despite the "tremendous bias against female players" and "awful" sexism prevalent in the 1970s, Chrissie Hynde persevered, using the "Free For All" attitude of punk to prove her guitar-playing abilities were on par with men, eventually becoming a role model herself. "The sexism was awful. But Chrissy fought through it and in the process became a role model herself."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation and UK Single Release
podcast.body: The Pretenders were formed by Chrissie Hynde in the late 1970s. They released their single "Brass in Pocket" in the UK in November 1979, as the decade was coming to a close. "Chrissy Hind formed the pretenders in the late 70s and just as the 70s were coming to an end in November 1979, the pretenders released this single in the UK."

srcs.source: For the Record - The 70s

podcast.title: Heroin Decimation
podcast.body: Heroin tragically decimated and brought death to the band members of The Pretenders. "Heroin decimated and brought death to the New York dolls. The pretenders sublime, smashing pumpkins, allyson chains, skinny puppy holes, Scott Wylin, D.D. Ramone, Billy Eidle, a chunk of ever-clear, a vast swath of the Britpop scene of the 1990s, and pretty much everyone who's ever been in the Red Hot Chili Peppers past in present."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Johnny Marr's Collaboration
podcast.body: After The Smiths broke up, Johnny Marr worked and toured with The Pretenders as a session guitarist, contributing to their music. "Johnny Mar became a very hot session guitarist, working in touring with the pretenders in Dada."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Modesty about Accomplishments
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde is noted for being modest about her achievements. In a 2016 interview, she linked music to the times it's made, implying the significance of "Brass in Pocket" as a reflection of progress for women in music, even if she didn't frame it as such herself. "It is also not at all unlike Chrissy Hind to be very modest about her accomplishments. In a 2016 interview, she said that music reflects the time that it's being made."

podcast.title: Move to London and Punk Scene Immersion
podcast.body: In her early 20s, Hynde moved from Akron, Ohio, to London, where she deeply engaged with the burgeoning early punk scene. She contributed writing to the music magazine The NME and frequently associated with figures from bands like the Sex Pistols and The Clash while trying to form her own band. "When she was in her early 20s, she moved from Akrona, Ohio to London and immersed herself in the early punk scene. She wrote for the Music Magazine, The NME, and she hung out with people like the sex pistols in the clash, while trying to get a band off the ground."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: New Wave Marketing
podcast.body: Sire Records successfully marketed The Pretenders under the New Wave banner, capitalizing on their unique blend of punk energy and pop sensibilities to broaden their audience appeal. "So it's no wonder that the pretenders were successfully marketed by Sire, of course, under the new wave banner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: North American Importation by Seymour Stein
podcast.body: The Pretenders were among the "unknown English bands" that legendary record executive Seymour Stein, founder of Sire Records, imported into North America, helping them gain exposure and a following. "He's the guy that imported unknown English bands like The Smiths and The Pretenders and The English Beat into North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Pop Song Appreciation
podcast.body: Despite her strong punk background, Chrissie Hynde also recognized and valued the appeal and power of a well-crafted pop song, integrating this sensibility into The Pretenders' music. "But she also appreciated the power and the value of a good pop song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Radio Success
podcast.body: The Pretenders were among the New Wave bands that found success on pop and rock radio, indicating their ability to cross over to mainstream audiences. "While some New Wave bands thrived on pop and rock radio, the pretenders, blondie, the cars, the police, among them, others struggled to find attention outside of their original circle of fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Recording at Wessex Studios
podcast.body: The Pretenders recorded at Wessex Studios, an old church hall in North London favored by punk and post-punk bands for its live sound. "A lot of punk bands and post punk bands, like using the place, the clash and the damned and suzy and the banshees and the pretenders and the specials and generation X and the sex pistols."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sid Vicious Marriage Attempt
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde notably almost married Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols, an attempt to acquire the British equivalent of a green card to remain in the UK. This anecdote further illustrates her deep connections within the early punk scene. "And then there was also the time that she nearly married Sid Vicious of the Sex Pistols just so she could stay in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Signed by Seymour Stein
podcast.body: The Pretenders were signed to Sire Records by its founder, Seymour Stein. Stein built a reputation for discovering and signing a wide range of pivotal artists, including many of the era's most important acts.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Signed to Sire Records
podcast.body: The Pretenders were signed to Sire Records, a New York record label established by Seymour Stein. "Sire Records, a New York record label that signed everyone from the remones to the talking heads, to the tragically hip, to the pretenders."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)" Advocacy
podcast.body: Chrissie Hynde, lead singer of The Pretenders and then married to Simple Minds singer Jim Kerr, played a crucial role in convincing Simple Minds to record "Don't You (Forget About Me)." Despite the band's reluctance to record an outsider's song, Hynde's intervention contributed to them reconsidering and ultimately recording what would become their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sire Records Endorsement
podcast.body: Seymour Stein, head of Sire Records, was drawn to The Pretenders, appreciating their edgy, punky sound, songwriting talent, and the image of a strong American woman (Chrissie Hynde) fronting a band that was 75% English, which he saw as the epitome of New Wave. "To him, it didn't get any more new wave than that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

podcast.title: Sire Records Signing
podcast.body: The Pretenders were among the post-punk bands from the UK and Ireland signed by Seymour Stein to Sire Records, indicating his commitment to this emerging sound. Sire Records used the term "New Wave" as a marketing tool for these acts in North America. "he was very, very into this new post-punk music coming out of the UK in Ireland, the pretenders."

xref.title: Conquest of England (July 4 & 6, 1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played two pivotal shows in London, first at the Roundhouse (capacity 2,000) on America's bicentennial, and then at Dingwalls two nights later. Despite their European record company trying to cancel gigs, the band delivered explosive performances. These concerts were England's "first proper exposure" to US-style punk rock and are credited with transforming nearly every major player in the burgeoning British punk rock scene, including members of the Sex Pistols, The Clash, The Pretenders, The Damned, and Generation X. "And over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th, 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Witnessing The Ramones (July 4, 1976)
xref.body: Members of the newly formed Clash, including Joe Strummer, were present at The Ramones' July 4, 1976 gig at the Roundhouse in London. Strummer recounted how they got backstage by forming a "human chain" through a window to meet The Ramones, describing it as a "really great punk rock moment." "Members of the newly formed clash, Chrissy Hind of the still unformed pretenders, the damn who would become the first British punk band to release a record, Generation X featuring a very young Billy Isle. They were all at these gigs and they were all transformed by what they saw and heard."

xref.title: Andy Rourke Death (May 18, 2023) – Pancreatic Cancer, Age 59; Sued Morrissey, Later Played Two Morrissey Singles
xref.body: Andy Rourke was a founding member of the Smiths and is considered by fans one of the greatest bassists in the history of British indie rock. His time with the band ended badly: a heroin addiction, a lawsuit against Morrissey and Johnny Marr for unpaid royalties (he was broke), and a decade later a bankruptcy over tax issues. Post-Smiths, he worked with the Pretenders, Killing Joke, Stone Roses singer Ian Brown, Dolores O'Riordan and the Cranberries, and Peter Hook of New Order. In a remarkable reconciliation, he played on two Morrissey solo singles despite the money disputes. His father and sister were both diagnosed with cancer, which prompted him to start a cancer charity; he himself was later diagnosed with pancreatic cancer. He died in a New York hospital on May 18, 2023, age 59. "Ask any Smiths fan, and they'll tell you that he was one of the greatest bassists in the history of British Indie Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Blackie O'Nassis Death (June 13, 2023) – Drummer on Pulp Fiction's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon"; Age 57, Cause Unknown
xref.body: John Rowan, who played under the name Blackie O'Nassis, was the drummer for Urge Overkill — the Chicago band whose cover of Neil Diamond's "Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon" (1967) appears in the famous dance scene in *Pulp Fiction*. The band was also a cult favorite in the alt-rock community and opened for Nirvana on the *Nevermind* tour, during which they befriended Kurt Cobain, Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders, and Liz Phair. Blackie left the band in 1996; there were reports of heroin use and at least one arrest. The cause of his death on June 13, 2023, at age 57 was never disclosed. "As for the cause of his death on June 13th, 2023, we have no idea."

xref.title: Advocate for Simple Minds
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde, lead singer of The Pretenders, played a crucial role in convincing Simple Minds to record "Don't You (Forget About Me)" for *The Breakfast Club* soundtrack. As the wife of Simple Minds' singer Jim Kerr at the time, she asked everyone in the band to reconsider their initial reluctance, which ultimately led them to record their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Akron Origin
xref.body: The Pretenders are mentioned in connection with Akron, Ohio, as the original home of Chrissy Hine, which is also the home of The Black Keys and a source of regional influence for Karen O. of The Ye-Eyes. "And just an hour away was Akron, the original home of Christy Hine and the pretenders, and the home of the Black Keys."

xref.body: The Pretenders finally solidified in 1978 after several earlier attempts by Chrissie Hynde to establish a band. "There were several before the pretenders finally took hold of 1978."

xref.title: Bridge Between Punk and New Wave
xref.body: The Pretenders were considered a crucial bridge, linking the raw energy of old-school punk with the evolving sounds of the New Wave era. "The pretenders were a crucial bridge between old school punk and the era of New Wave."

xref.title: Chrissie Hynde Association
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde of The Pretenders worked in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop during the Sex Pistols' formative years. She also famously considered marrying Sid Vicious, the band's bassist, primarily to secure the British equivalent of a green card and remain in the UK. "Along with working in Malcolm McLaren's clothing shop in the earliest days of the Sex Pistols, she also wrote about punk in one of the British music magazines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Chrissie Hynde Collaboration
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde, frontwoman of The Pretenders, was one of the artists who collaborated with Taylor Hawkins on his Co-Tale Riders albums. Her involvement underscores the diverse range of musicians Hawkins brought into his side project. "Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders."

xref.title: Evolution from London SS
xref.body: The Clash evolved out of a prominent British punk band known as the London SS, which was famous for never playing a gig. Many musicians passed through London SS, including Chrissie Hynde, who later formed The Pretenders. "The Clash evolved out of the most famous British punk band to never play a gig. They were called the London SS."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Exotic Appeal
xref.body: The fact that three-quarters of The Pretenders' members were English contributed to the band's somewhat exotic appeal, adding a distinctive touch to their image and sound within the New Wave landscape. "Add in the fact that the pretenders were three quarters English, also gave them a somewhat exotic touch."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Founding The Pretenders – Lead Woman in Rock
xref.body: After several attempts to form a band, including discussions with Mick Jones before he formed The Clash, Chrissie Hynde founded The Pretenders in 1978. She was unique in late 1970s rock as a woman who not only sang lead and fronted the band but also played rhythm guitar and wrote most of their music, thriving in the receptive British punk environment. "Chrissy formed the pretenders in 1978. Here we have a woman singing lead, acting as front person and spokesperson and playing with in guitar. Not exactly a common thing in rock in the late 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Kurt Cobain's Acknowledged Influence
xref.body: The Raincoats were an all-female post-punk band often named by Kurt Cobain as a significant influence, making them an initial inspiration for the Riot Grrrl movement. Their work was cited alongside other pioneering female artists in punk and post-punk. "They were the raincoats, an all-female post-punk band that were often named Jack by Kurt Cobain, Kim Gordon of Sonic Youth, goth queen Suzy Su, Chrissy Hine to the pretenders, Exine Servenka of the LA punk band X."

Their home city of Akron, Ohio, is also highlighted as the original home of Chrissie Hynde and The Pretenders, and a regional influence for Karen O. of the Ye-Eyes. "And just an hour away was Akron, the original home of Christy Hine and the pretenders, and the home of the Black Keys."

Hynde's personal appeal to the band was instrumental in convincing them to record the song, which became their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

xref.title: Marriage to Seymour Stein - Sire Records Connection
xref.body: Linda was married to Seymour Stein, the founder of Sire Records. This New York record label signed influential artists such as The Ramones, Talking Heads, The Tragically Hip, The Pretenders, and Madonna. "She was also married to see more Stein, the founder of Sire Records, a New York record label that signed everyone from the remones to the talking heads, to the tragically hip, to the pretenders to Madonna."

xref.title: New Wave Marketing
xref.body: Sire Records successfully marketed The Pretenders under the New Wave banner, capitalizing on their unique blend of punk energy and pop sensibilities to broaden their audience appeal. "So it's no wonder that the pretenders were successfully marketed by Sire, of course, under the new wave banner."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New Wave Success
xref.body: Blondie was among the New Wave bands that successfully navigated mainstream pop and rock radio, thriving in the post-punk era. "While some New Wave bands thrived on pop and rock radio, the pretenders, blondie, the cars, the police, among them, others struggled to find attention outside of their original circle of fans."

srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: New York Formation and Midwest Influences
xref.body: Singer Karen O. and drummer Brian Chase met at college in Ohio in the late 1990s. They later moved to New York, where they met photographer and guitarist Nick Zinner. Their initial band, Unitarred, evolved its sound to incorporate the "trashy, punky Garage Rock" Karen O. heard in Ohio, drawing influences from Detroit (140 miles up I-90) and Cleveland (35 miles east on Highway 10), near Akron (home of The Pretenders and The Black Keys). "Singer Karen O. met drummer Brian Chase at College in Ohio in the late 1990s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

xref.title: North American Importation by Seymour Stein
xref.body: The Smiths were one of several unknown English bands imported into North America by legendary record executive Seymour Stein, who was the founder of Sire Records. Stein was instrumental in bringing their music to a wider audience. "He's the guy that imported unknown English bands like The Smiths and The Pretenders and The English Beat into North America."

xref.title: Pop Song Appreciation
xref.body: Despite her strong punk background, Chrissie Hynde also recognized and valued the appeal and power of a well-crafted pop song, integrating this sensibility into The Pretenders' music. "But she also appreciated the power and the value of a good pop song."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Smiths Career as Session Guitarist
xref.body: After The Smiths' breakup, Johnny Marr became a highly sought-after session guitarist. He worked and toured with The Pretenders and Dada, and later co-founded Electronic with Barney Sumner of New Order. He also became a friend and confidante of Noel Gallagher of Oasis, collaborating with him in the studio, and worked with artists like Beth Orton, Neil Finn, Paul McCartney, and Talking Heads. "Meanwhile, Johnny Mar became a very hot session guitarist, working in touring with the pretenders in Dada."

xref.title: Punk Pioneer
xref.body: Siouxsie Sioux of Siouxsie and the Banshees was a pioneer who took advantage of punk rock values, inspiring many to express themselves regardless of background or gender. "Suzy Su, of Suzy in the Banshee's, members of the Slitz, Pauli Styrene of X-Ray Specks, Chrissy Hinder, the Pretenders, Patty Smith, and so many more. They were all pioneers and they all inspired many people, women, but also men, to do what they did."

xref.title: Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)" Advocacy
xref.body: Chrissie Hynde, lead singer of The Pretenders and then married to Simple Minds singer Jim Kerr, played a crucial role in convincing Simple Minds to record "Don't You (Forget About Me)." Despite the band's reluctance to record an outsider's song, Hynde's intervention contributed to them reconsidering and ultimately recording what would become their biggest hit. "But the label kept up the pressure and Chrissy Holland at the pretenders, who was married to Singer Jim Carr at the time, asked everyone in the band to reconsider."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sire Records Endorsement
xref.body: Seymour Stein, head of Sire Records, was drawn to The Pretenders, appreciating their edgy, punky sound, songwriting talent, and the image of a strong American woman (Chrissie Hynde) fronting a band that was 75% English, which he saw as the epitome of New Wave. "To him, it didn't get any more new wave than that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 1: New Wave

xref.title: Sire Records Signing
xref.body: The Pretenders were among the post-punk bands from the UK and Ireland signed by Seymour Stein to Sire Records, indicating his commitment to this emerging sound. Sire Records used the term "New Wave" as a marketing tool for these acts in North America. "he was very, very into this new post-punk music coming out of the UK in Ireland, the pretenders."
